case.holding: Scraping data that a website makes publicly available without any login does not amount to access without authorisation under the CFAA.
case.case_name: hiQ Labs, Inc. v. LinkedIn Corp.

case.why_ai_cites_it: The principal authority that collecting public web data is not a federal computer crime, which is the first hurdle any web-scale training corpus has to clear.

reading.body:
The Ninth Circuit's 2022 ruling in hiQ v. LinkedIn remains the principal federal authority that scraping publicly accessible web data is not a crime under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, which matters directly to anyone assembling a web-scale AI training corpus.

The holding is narrow in a way that practitioners must not overlook. It resolves only the CFAA question. Contract claims, trespass to chattels, copyright, and state privacy theories remain fully available to a platform that wants to block a scraper, and LinkedIn subsequently prevailed against hiQ on contract grounds. A company that clears the CFAA hurdle has cleared one gate, not the whole fence.

For AI development, the CFAA question is nonetheless the first gate, because a federal criminal or civil liability finding would make large-scale public-web collection untenable regardless of any other consideration. The case does not speak to whether scraped data may be used to train a model, whether doing so infringes copyright, or whether any infrastructure built on such data is compliant with platform terms. Two live cases involving Amazon and Perplexity AI indicate that downstream questions about what scrapers do with collected data are still being litigated. What hiQ settles is the threshold: access itself, where no login is required, is not unauthorized access under federal law.
